title: Linearizability, serializability and the consistency zoo
problem: Alice sees the final score, tells Bob, and Bob's refresh still shows the match in progress because his read hit a replica that had not caught up.
summary: Linearizability makes replicated data behave like one copy in real time; serializability makes concurrent transactions equivalent to some serial order; strict serializability is both. Reserve the top of the map for locks, uniqueness and leaders, because it costs round trips and availability.
catTip: One food bowl, one truth: when it is empty, it is empty for every cat, instantly. Two bowls that are usually the same are how the kitten eats twice. Linearizability is the one-bowl illusion, and it costs a walk to the kitchen.

recall.q: What is the difference between linearizability and serializability, and what do you call having both?
recall.a: Linearizability is a single-object, single-operation guarantee that every operation appears to take effect instantly between its call and its return, so reads reflect real time. Serializability is a multi-object transaction guarantee of equivalence to some serial order, with no real-time requirement. Both together is strict serializability, which Spanner calls external consistency.

guide.breaks: Without linearizability two nodes can both read free and both take the last seat or the lock, and a user can be told a fact by a friend that their own refresh then denies.
guide.tradeoffs: Every linearizable read or write goes through a leader or quorum round trip and must refuse or wait during a partition, so the guarantee is bought per object, not for the whole system.
guide.explainSimply: Imagine a scoreboard that every fan in the stadium sees at the same instant: when it changes, nobody can still see the old score. Weaker promises are like news spreading through a crowd, where everyone eventually hears the result but some people hear it later than their friends. Linearizability is the single-scoreboard promise, and it needs everyone to check with the scoreboard rather than the crowd.
guide.hint: Think about which guarantee mentions real time, which mentions transactions, and the name for the one that does both.

meow: One bowl, one truth, every whisker sees the same emptiness at once. Many bowls, meow-ny truths, and the kitten eats twice.

quiz.prompt: A database runs every transaction at SERIALIZABLE isolation but serves read-only transactions from a replica that is a few seconds behind. Which statement is correct?
options: The system is linearizable, because serializable is the strongest isolation level
The system is serializable but not strictly serializable: the serial order it is equivalent to need not match real time, so a read can miss a write that completed before it began
The system is strictly serializable, because each replica applies transactions in commit order
The system is neither serializable nor linearizable, because stale reads violate isolation
quiz.explanation: Serializability only requires equivalence to some serial order, so an old snapshot is allowed, and adding the real-time requirement is what makes it strict. Applying writes in order on each replica does not help, because a read can land on a replica that has not yet applied them.

options: The follower count shown on a profile page
Comments in a thread appearing after the post they reply to
Allocating the last seat in a show to exactly one of two simultaneous buyers
A user seeing their own just-posted comment on refresh
quiz.explanation: Exactly one winner requires both buyers' operations to behave as if on a single copy in real time, so the second sees the seat taken. The comments case needs only causal ordering and seeing your own write needs only read-your-writes, both of which are cheaper.

cards.q: Give an example of a system that is serializable but not linearizable.
cards.a: A database at SERIALIZABLE isolation that serves read-only transactions from a slightly stale snapshot. Each such read is equivalent to a serial order in which it ran earlier, so serializability holds, but a write that completed before the read started is invisible, so real-time (linearizable) order is broken.

cards.q: Why does linearizability cost latency and availability?
cards.a: A linearizable read must be served by a leader or by a quorum guaranteed to include the latest write, and a write must wait for that quorum, so each costs at least one network round trip. During a partition a cut-off node cannot know whether a newer write exists, so it must refuse or wait rather than answer.

sources.title: Maurice Herlihy and Jeannette Wing, "Linearizability: A Correctness Condition for Concurrent Objects", ACM TOPLAS 12(3), 1990, pp. 463–492
sources.supports: the 1990 definition and attribution of linearizability (bibliographic record checked via Crossref; only scanned copies were reachable, so the text was not re-read)

sources.title: Jepsen, "Consistency Models" reference
sources.supports: the hierarchy of models organised as Models, Phenomena and Dependencies, with models defined by the dependency cycles they forbid

sources.title: Jepsen, "Linearizability"
sources.supports: operations appear to take place atomically in an order consistent with real time; a single-object model; cannot be totally or sticky available

sources.title: Jepsen, "Strict Serializability"
sources.supports: strict serializability implies both serializability and linearizability and is not totally or sticky available

sources.title: Jepsen, "Serializability"
sources.supports: serializability imposes no real-time or per-process constraints, so a read is not guaranteed to observe an earlier completed write; not totally or sticky available

sources.title: Jepsen, "Sequential Consistency"
sources.supports: a total order consistent with each process's order, attributed to Lamport 1979; cannot be totally or sticky available

sources.title: Jepsen, "Causal Consistency"
sources.supports: causally related operations appear in the same order on all processes; processes may disagree about the order of causally independent operations; causal consistency is sticky available

sources.title: Peter Bailis, "Linearizability versus Serializability" (24 September 2014)
sources.supports: linearizability as a single-operation, single-object, real-time guarantee; serializability as a multi-object guarantee with no real-time order; strict serializability as the combination; the C in CAP being linearizability per Gilbert and Lynch; neither achievable without coordination

sources.title: Corbett et al., "Spanner: Google's Globally-Distributed Database", OSDI 2012
sources.supports: Spanner's serialization order satisfies external consistency, which the paper equates with linearizability: if T1 commits before T2 starts, T1's commit timestamp is smaller

sources.title: Christos Papadimitriou, "The serializability of concurrent database updates", Journal of the ACM 26(4), 1979
sources.supports: the formal definition of serializability (bibliographic record checked; text not re-read)

sources.title: Leslie Lamport, "How to Make a Multiprocessor Computer That Correctly Executes Multiprocess Programs", IEEE Transactions on Computers C-28(9), 1979
sources.supports: the origin of sequential consistency (bibliographic record checked; text not re-read)

sources.title: Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch, "Brewer's conjecture and the feasibility of consistent, available, partition-tolerant web services", ACM SIGACT News 33(2), 2002
sources.supports: the CAP proof whose consistency is linearizability (bibliographic record checked; text not re-read)
